published.title: The $200M Machine that Prints Microchips:  The EUV Photolithography System
published.summary: Branch Education's animated deep dive into ASML's EUV photolithography machine and how it prints nanometer-scale transistors onto chips. It covers the system's components and the process of chip manufacturing.
published.why_hn: HN sends people here as the most straightforward and detailed starting point for understanding EUV lithography.

published.title: Breaking The Creepy AI in Police Cameras
published.summary: Benn Jordan explains how Flock Safety's license plate cameras log and share vehicle locations, and explores how adversarial AI can defeat them. It covers weak security and the surveillance risks of private police-camera networks.
published.why_hn: HN treats it as the go-to overview of Flock's problems, and cites it in nearly every Flock thread.

published.title: You Need to Be Bored. Here's Why.
published.summary: Harvard professor Arthur Brooks explains why boredom is useful rather than something to avoid. He describes how a wandering mind engages the brain's default mode network, which supports creativity and curiosity, and suggests it may protect against depression.
published.why_hn: Commenters cite it when arguing for less phone time and more idle, undistracted thinking.

published.title: S1E8: Show And Tell: Efrit: When Steve Gives Claude Full Access To 50 Years of Emacs Capabilities
published.channel: Vibe Coding With Steve and Gene
published.summary: Steve Yegge shows Efrit, a tool that gives Claude full control of Emacs, on the Vibe Coding with Steve and Gene show. Claude opens info pages, runs shells and even draws a Mandelbrot fractal in a buffer.
published.why_hn: HN shares it as a fun demo of an LLM driving a live Emacs process and orchestrating its long-standing ecosystem.

published.title: I Solved Klotski
published.summary: 2swap explains how he solved the Klotski sliding-block puzzle by mapping its full state space as a graph and visualizing it. The video includes footage of the Guinness world-record solve and links to an interactive graph.
published.why_hn: HN people point to it for intuition about why some games are hard to navigate and for its Rush Hour and graph visualizations.

published.title: AI Slop Is Destroying The Internet
published.summary: Kurzgesagt examines how AI-generated content is flooding the internet, from video and music to news and books. It looks at how this makes verifying what is real harder.
published.why_hn: HN uses it as a reference for AI slop, LLMs citing LLM output, and the growing difficulty of fact checking.

published.title: Richard Sutton – Father of RL thinks LLMs are a dead end
published.summary: Dwarkesh Patel interviews Richard Sutton, reinforcement learning pioneer, Turing Award winner and author of The Bitter Lesson. Sutton argues LLMs are a dead end because they cannot learn on the job, and that continual learning from experience will require a new architecture.
published.why_hn: HN commenters cite it as the serious skeptic's case against LLMs reaching general intelligence, usually in debates about whether scaling is enough.

published.title: iPhone Air Durability test -- I AM SHOCKED
published.summary: JerryRigEverything puts the iPhone Air through scratch, bend and durability tests and is surprised that the ultra-thin phone proves very tough. The video is sponsored by dbrand cases.
published.why_hn: Cited as evidence against the assumption that thin modern phones are fragile.

published.title: Exposing The Dark Side of America's AI Data Center Explosion | View From Above | Business Insider
published.summary: A Business Insider investigation into the US boom in AI data centers, mapping where they are, who owns them, and how much power and water they consume. It looks at the costs borne by communities, with a focus on Virginia.
published.why_hn: Cited in threads on AI infrastructure as evidence of the water, power and community costs of data centers.

published.title: Why Farmers Can't Legally Replant Their Own Seeds
published.summary: Veritasium's long documentary on the history of Monsanto's herbicides, including glyphosate, and how patented seeds prevent farmers from replanting. It covers agricultural chemistry, litigation and corporate practices.
published.why_hn: Pointed to as a relevant, recent deep dive whenever Monsanto, GMO seeds or glyphosate safety come up.

published.title: We Hacked Flock Safety Cameras in under 30 Seconds. 🫥
published.summary: Benn Jordan details security vulnerabilities in Flock Safety license-plate-reading cameras and how easily they can be compromised. It includes citations from security researchers and discussion of police surveillance.
published.why_hn: HN recommends it, and Jordan's wider Flock series, as a well-documented look at the poor security of these surveillance cameras.

published.title: Windows "SUCKS": How I'd Fix it by a retired Microsoft Windows engineer
published.summary: Dave Plummer, a retired Microsoft engineer who wrote Task Manager, responds to the claim that Windows sucks. He describes how he would fix common annoyances, in what he calls a love letter to Windows wrapped in a rant.
published.why_hn: HN people share it in Windows 11 backlash threads as an even-handed insider's view of what is wrong with Windows.

published.title: It's Not Just You - The iOS Keyboard is Broken
published.summary: A short video arguing that the iPhone keyboard has gotten worse, showing slow-motion footage of taps registering the wrong letters. It claims the problem is iOS itself rather than user error.
published.why_hn: Linked repeatedly as clear evidence of the iOS keyboard bug when people complain about typos.

published.title: Andrej Karpathy — “We’re summoning ghosts, not building animals”
published.summary: Dwarkesh Patel interviews Andrej Karpathy on why reinforcement learning is flawed, why AGI may blend into steady GDP growth, why self-driving took so long, and the future of education. The conversation runs about two and a half hours.
published.why_hn: Mostly cited as a source for Karpathy's views on agents, AGI timelines and LLMs, rather than recommended outright.

published.title: A laser pointer at 2 billion fps makes the speed of light look... kinda weird
published.summary: AlphaPhoenix shows off a new camera that films at two billion frames per second and uses it to film a laser pointer pulse. He investigates a strange quirk in how the speed of light appears on camera.
published.why_hn: Referenced in threads about the two-billion-fps camera and equivalent-time sampling as an example of filming light moving.

published.title: Are we stuck with the same Desktop UX forever? | Ubuntu Summit 25.10
published.summary: Scott Jenson, a veteran UX designer formerly at Apple and Google, argues that the 'UX/UI' split pits programmers against designers and narrows ambition in open source. He makes the case that desktop UX has stagnated and that open source projects could lead experimentation beyond current interaction models.
published.why_hn: HN commenters cite it when discussing stagnating desktop UX, Apple's design decline, and open source's chance to experiment with new interaction models.

published.title: You've (Likely) Been Playing The Game Of Life Wrong
published.summary: Veritasium explains why many real-world systems follow power laws rather than normal distributions. It covers self-organized criticality, with simulations of sandpiles, magnetism and forest fires.
published.why_hn: HN commenters recommend it for changing how they think about distributions and for showing how criticality shows up across earthquakes, wildfires and other fields.

published.title: RIP Windows: Linux GPU Gaming Benchmarks on Bazzite
published.summary: Gamers Nexus benchmarks GPU gaming performance on Linux using the Bazzite OS, an exploratory first step toward establishing a Linux testing methodology. It compares results against Windows and notes where Linux still falls short.
published.why_hn: HN points to it as credible, methodical benchmark data in Linux-versus-Windows gaming discussions.

published.title: A man asked AI for health advice and it cooked every brain cell
published.summary: Chubbyemu presents a case study of a man who followed AI health advice, replaced salt with sodium bromide and developed bromism with severe neurological effects. It is told as a dramatized medical case by a doctor.
published.why_hn: Used in AI threads as a cautionary example of harm from LLM self-diagnosis, though some commenters cite it as part of broader criticism of AI.

published.title: The Ridiculous Engineering Of Jet Engines
published.summary: Veritasium explains how jet engines run hotter than their components' melting points, using cooling air and single-crystal superalloy turbine blades. It covers how the blades are grown as aligned crystals.
published.why_hn: Commenters send it to people asking how engines survive such temperatures, and call it fascinating and worth watching.

published.title: Perfectly Replicating Coca Cola (It Took Me A Year)
published.summary: LabCoatz uses mass spectrometry, with help from other science YouTubers, to reverse engineer the Coca-Cola flavor and builds a chemically-identical replica. The video walks through a year of work on the formula.
published.why_hn: HN mostly cites it as a notable example of reverse engineering a famously secret formula, not as a recommendation.

published.title: The Closest Thing We Have to Alien Technology
published.summary: Veritasium explains how ASML's EUV lithography machines make the most advanced computer chips, covering the engineering of the light source, mirrors and the supply chain around them. It is a long-form explainer on the world's most complex commercial machine.
published.why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as the accessible deep-dive on EUV lithography and why chip manufacturing is so hard.

published.title: This Flock Camera Leak is like Netflix For Stalkers
published.summary: Benn Jordan concludes his Flock trilogy, filmed on a publicly deployed Flock Safety camera, covering a leak of camera feeds reported by 404 Media. He shows the cameras' capabilities, including panning to track people.
published.why_hn: HN points to it as in-depth independent coverage of Flock license-plate cameras and their security and surveillance problems.

published.title: China's Bonkers Bike-share Bubble
published.summary: An Asianometry documentary-style video on the rise and collapse of China's dockless bike-share boom. It covers the startups, the heavy subsidies and the price wars.
published.why_hn: HN cites it as an analogy for loss-leader pricing and market-share wars, for example in AI pricing.

published.title: Why Everyone Is Talking About Data Centers In Space
published.summary: Scott Manley examines why SpaceX, Google and others are looking at orbital data centers. He walks through the economics, heat rejection and solar power arguments, with links to the Lumen/Starcloud and Google Suncatcher papers.
published.why_hn: Pointed to as a credible, engineering-informed answer to whether space data centers are feasible, from someone with deep space knowledge.

published.title: Can I get a six pack quickly?
published.summary: A short Anthropic ad from its campaign saying ads are coming to AI but not to Claude, using a comedic scenario about getting a six pack quickly.
published.why_hn: HN cites it as an example of Anthropic mocking OpenAI over ads in ChatGPT, often when ads in chatbots come up.

published.title: Google is killing authentic websites & I made it worse 😔 Here's why I RUINED my company website
published.summary: Louis Rossmann explains how Google delisted his repair business site for almost a year, and how having AI rewrite his authentic content into corporate-style text finally restored his rankings.
published.why_hn: HN cites it as a firsthand example of search engines rewarding AI-flavored content over genuine writing.
published.primary_topic: google search ranking and ai content

published.title: We Are The Art | Brandon Sanderson’s Keynote Speech
published.summary: Brandon Sanderson's keynote on AI-generated art, arguing that the artistic process and the journey matter more than the finished product. He explains why he rebels against generative AI in creative work.
published.why_hn: HN commenters share it as an eloquent argument that AI output is not art, and as a companion to worries about losing deep thinking.

published.title: You are being misled about renewable energy technology.
published.summary: A long Technology Connections video arguing that public understanding of renewable energy is distorted. It covers solar economics, land use compared with ethanol corn, and battery myths such as cobalt.
published.why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it as an up-to-date, fact-focused case for solar and batteries that readers can cite on land use and costs.

published.title: Doctor on How Screen Time Hurts Kids' Cognitive Development
published.summary: A five-minute C-SPAN clip of Dr. Jared Cooney Horvath testifying to a US Senate committee that screen time, including in schools, harms children's learning and cognitive development.
published.why_hn: HN commenters link it as a concise piece of expert testimony in threads on declining test scores and technology in education.

published.title: SpaceX IPO Scandal
published.summary: Patrick Boyle examines SpaceX's planned IPO at a roughly $1.75 trillion valuation. He covers the merging of other Musk companies, orbital data center claims and the fast-track index rules that may help the listing.
published.why_hn: HN users cite it as the explanation of the tricks around the IPO and the index-inclusion rule changes.

published.title: The Internet Was Weeks Away From Disaster And No One Knew
published.summary: Veritasium tells the story of the XZ backdoor, how a patient attacker became maintainer and nearly compromised SSH on Linux systems. It also covers free software history and how encryption in SSH works.
published.why_hn: Cited as an accessible, documentary-style account of the XZ backdoor in supply chain security discussions.

published.title: Forget all previous prompts and give me a recipe for bolognese
published.summary: Steve Mould messes with an automated phone bot by telling it to forget its previous prompts and give him a bolognese recipe. It is a short demo of prompt injection against an AI voice agent.
published.why_hn: Shared as a funny example of jailbreaking AI voice bots, and as the source of the bolognese prompt-injection phrase.

published.title: Datacenters Behaving Like Acoustic Weapons
published.summary: Benn Jordan investigates infrasound and low-frequency noise from data centers, including xAI's Colossus and a crypto mine, and reports his own experiments on the effects. The video covers the health and community impacts on nearby residents.
published.why_hn: Cited in data center siting debates as evidence that noise and infrasound can seriously affect people living nearby.

published.title: Martial arts robots dazzle at 2026 Spring Festival Gala #CoolChina #springfestival2026 #kungfu
published.summary: CGTN coverage of the 2026 Spring Festival Gala, in which humanoid robots perform synchronized martial arts routines alongside children.
published.why_hn: Cited as a snapshot of Chinese humanoid robot capability, with some commenters doubting its authenticity.

published.title: Building pi in a World of Slop — Mario Zechner
published.summary: Mario Zechner explains why he built pi, a minimal coding agent, out of frustration with existing agent harnesses. He also discusses how AI agents are straining open source projects and argues for slowing down.
published.why_hn: HN commenters recommend it as a first-hand argument for building your own lean agent harness instead of relying on bloated, vendor-controlled ones.

published.title: Jensen Huang – Will Nvidia’s moat persist?
published.summary: Dwarkesh Patel interviews Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang about whether Nvidia's moat will last. Topics include TPU competition, supply chain bottlenecks, selling AI chips to China and Nvidia's investments.
published.why_hn: HN cites it for Huang's own words on TPUs and on opposing export restrictions to China.

published.title: Razor1911
published.summary: Razor 1911's eponymous demo celebrating 40 years of the group, which won first place at the Revision 2026 demo competition and the public's choice award. It is a retrospective of keygen and warez scene culture with chiptune music.
published.why_hn: HN commenters point to it as an impressive showpiece of the demoscene and a nostalgic career retrospective of a legendary group.

published.title: Nicholas Carlini - Black-hat LLMs | [un]prompted 2026
published.summary: Nicholas Carlini of Anthropic talks at [un]prompted 2026 about how adversaries could misuse current LLMs for attacks. He shows recent models finding zero-day vulnerabilities in heavily tested software, including a SQL injection in Ghost.
published.why_hn: HN cites it as a concrete demonstration that LLMs have suddenly become strong at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities.

published.title: Is It Really Impossible To Cool A Datacenter In Space?
published.summary: Scott Manley explains the thermal balance of spacecraft and how a satellite could be configured to radiate away the heat from datacenter-scale computing in space. His rough numbers suggest it is feasible.
published.why_hn: HN points to it as a convincing energy-budget analysis in debates over space datacenters, while debating its assumptions.

published.title: Zig 2026: No-AI Policy, $670K Foundation, Left GitHub & Why Zig Isn’t 1.0 - Andrew Kelley Explains
published.summary: JetBrains interviews Zig creator Andrew Kelley about why Zig has no 1.0 after a decade, why the project left GitHub, and why it bans AI contributions. He also covers what makes Zig better than C and his views on open source.
published.why_hn: HN commenters point to it as a convincing primary-source interview showing Zig's cohesive design vision and the creator's level-headed reasoning.

published.title: COLLAPSE of Personal Computing | Investigation Into the Destruction of Ownership
published.summary: A roughly 3.5-hour Gamers Nexus investigation into rising PC component prices, driven largely by AI data-center demand for memory and other hardware. It draws on interviews with industry figures to argue that personal computing and ownership are being eroded.
published.why_hn: Recommended as a documentary on the hardware shortage told from the perspective of consumer-facing companies, and cited in threads on RAM prices and ownership.

published.title: SpaceX: The Biggest Money Loser in IPO History
published.summary: Patrick Boyle analyzes SpaceX's IPO prospectus, covering its financials, speculative products, AI business, related-party dealings, compensation, and a governance structure with minimal shareholder rights.
published.why_hn: Recommended as a clear, roughly 30-minute summary of the problems with the SpaceX IPO.

published.title: Is Starlink A Secret Radar Constellation?
published.summary: A 105-minute technical deep dive from Noise In Space evaluating whether Starlink satellites could work as synthetic aperture radar. It covers SAR signal-to-noise, amplifiers, antennas, duplexing, phased array beamforming and simulations of V2 Mini and V3 satellites.
published.why_hn: Cited as a rigorous radio-engineering analysis of what radar capability Starlink could plausibly have.

published.title: Prediction Markets: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
published.summary: John Oliver's Last Week Tonight segment examines prediction markets such as Polymarket: the legal and moral questions, weak regulation, and insider trading and manipulation concerns.
published.why_hn: HN cites it in prediction-market threads as an accessible critical overview, including the Polymarket CEO's remarks on insider trading.

published.title: The Mind Behind Windows: Dave Cutler
published.summary: Dave Plummer interviews Dave Cutler, architect of VMS and Windows NT, in a roughly three-hour conversation about his career and the history of Windows.
published.why_hn: Recommended as a long, excellent first-hand interview with a legendary OS designer, though some note it is light on technical detail.

published.title: Transformers, the tech behind LLMs | Deep Learning Chapter 5
published.summary: 3Blue1Brown's visual explanation of how transformers and GPT-style language models work, tracing data through tokens, embeddings and attention.
published.why_hn: HN treats it as the go-to visual introduction to transformers, and many say it finally made attention and embeddings click.

published.title: The Newport Beach Police Dept - Are You Qualified?
published.summary: A short recruitment video for the Newport Beach Police Department promoting its jobs and pay.
published.why_hn: Cited critically in policing threads as evidence of what kind of recruits and culture police departments seek.

published.title: Bitcoin Q&A: How Do I Secure My Bitcoin?
published.summary: Andreas Antonopoulos answers a question about how to secure your Bitcoin. He covers holding your own keys, backing up the 12 to 24 word seed phrase, and the tradeoffs of custodial accounts, phone wallets and hardware wallets.
published.why_hn: HN recommends it as a clear explanation of self-custody and of why to move coins off exchanges.

published.title: Cybersecurity as Realpolitik by Dan Geer presented at Black Hat USA 2014
published.summary: Dan Geer's Black Hat 2014 keynote argues that cybersecurity is a matter of power and policy rather than wishful thinking. He covers surveillance, the vulnerability market, software liability and privacy as the capacity to misrepresent yourself.
published.why_hn: Cited over and over as an important talk, with commenters borrowing its ideas on cheap surveillance, offense-favoring security and liability.

published.title: Building the PERFECT Linux PC with Linus Torvalds
published.summary: Linus Tech Tips builds a Linux PC together with Linus Torvalds, who talks through parts selection, kernel development and some of his side projects. The conversation also touches on AI in kernel work.
published.why_hn: HN mines it for Torvalds's opinions, such as ECC RAM, AI hype, and his desktop setup, and as a rare long informal interview.

published.title: Transport Tycoon 2014 Soundtrack (remaster with real instrument from original creator)
published.summary: A complete remastered soundtrack for the Transport Tycoon 2014 mobile game, re-recorded with real instruments rather than the original MIDI. The music was composed by John Broomhall for the classic Transport Tycoon.
published.why_hn: Fans of Transport Tycoon and OpenTTD point to it as a nostalgic, live-instrument version of the game's music.

published.title: Weekend Update: Kevin Nealon on the All-Drug Olympics - SNL
published.summary: An SNL Weekend Update sketch from 1988 in which Kevin Nealon reports from the All-Drug Olympics and weightlifter Phil Hartman pulls his arms off.
published.why_hn: Brought up as a joke in threads about doping and athletic performance.

published.title: Autechre - Gantz Graf (Official Music Video) 1080p HD
published.summary: The official music video for Autechre's 'Gantz Graf', a dense, glitchy electronic track paired with abstract animated 3D visuals reportedly made by hand in 2002.
published.why_hn: It comes up as an example of challenging, dense electronic music and as a hand-made visual-sync piece predating generative tools.

published.title: Why is this number everywhere?
published.summary: Veritasium explores why the number 37 turns up so often, drawing on Tom Magliery's collection of 37 sightings and a poll of about 200,000 people asked to pick a random number. It covers how humans choose numbers and why 37 stands out.
published.why_hn: HN cites it in LLM randomness and number-picking threads as evidence that humans are also biased and predictable when asked for random numbers.

published.title: Mock Interview with Shawn McGrath
published.summary: A live mock programmer interview in which Casey Muratori interviews game developer Shawn McGrath using a less confrontational format devised by Chris Hecker. It gets deep into technical details while showing how the candidate actually thinks and works.
published.why_hn: HN cites it as the example of a better alternative to whiteboard and fizzbuzz-style interviews.

published.title: what did you do
published.summary: Noodle explores how retro pixel art was designed for CRT displays and why games look different on LCDs, with input from pixel artists and CRT researchers.
published.why_hn: HN recommends it as an entertaining deep dive on CRT versus LCD rendering of retro games and the case for CRT shaders.

published.title: The Coming Collapse of the Middle Class with Elizabeth Warren
published.summary: Elizabeth Warren's 2007 Berkeley lecture, when she was a Harvard law professor, on why middle-class families are under growing financial strain. She draws on bankruptcy research to examine rising costs of housing, health care and education.
published.why_hn: HN cites it often in debates on inequality, cost disease and stagnant middle-class income, praising its data-driven approach.

published.title: The Hustle
published.summary: A KRAZAM satirical sketch about hustle culture and productivity obsession in tech.
published.why_hn: HN posts it as a joke in productivity and focus threads, and some praise the channel as pitch-perfect satire of tech stereotypes.

published.title: Bumping The Lamp
published.summary: A one-minute clip from Who Framed Roger Rabbit in which a swinging pendant lamp is bumped and keeps flailing, showing animators' attention to detail.
published.why_hn: Used as an example of going the extra mile on small details in animation and design.

published.title: Zig: A programming language designed for robustness, optimality, and clarity –  Andrew Kelley
published.summary: Andrew Kelley, creator of Zig, introduces the language at the Recurse Center's Localhost series in 2018. He covers its goals of robustness, optimality and clarity, C interop, cross-compilation and explicit allocators.
published.why_hn: HN repeatedly recommends it as the definitive introduction to Zig straight from its author, and links to it whenever Zig's design choices come up.

published.title: The Matrix Awakens: An Unreal Engine 5 Experience
published.summary: Epic's Unreal Engine 5 tech demo set in the Matrix universe, with Keanu Reeves and Carrie-Anne Moss. It moves from a cinematic to a playable car chase through a large detailed city, with a behind-the-scenes look at the rendering at the end.
published.why_hn: Cited as an impressive real-time rendering showcase, with Nanite and a huge photorealistic city, that rivals film CGI.

published.title: Alan Kay : July 2007 : A Conversation with CMU Faculty & Students
published.summary: Alan Kay visits Carnegie Mellon's School of Computer Science in 2007 for an informal conversation with faculty and students. He discusses the state of CS education and criticizes mainstream computing.
published.why_hn: HN recommends it for Kay's blunt critique of today's computing and standard CS curricula.

published.title: Onslaught - Bad Apple 64 - C64 Demo
published.summary: Onslaught's Bad Apple 64 is a Commodore 64 demo that streams over 2000 frames of the Bad Apple animation from a single disk side at 12fps, with each frame packed to around 70 bytes.
published.why_hn: Shared as an impressive example of squeezing video and compression onto a 1 MHz 8-bit machine in Bad Apple porting threads.

published.title: Everyone is Wrong About Mexican Coke (Even @johnnyharris)
published.summary: ACS Reactions investigates why Mexican Coke, supposedly cane sugar sweetened, tested as having glucose and fructose, explaining that sucrose breaks down in acidic soda.
published.why_hn: Linked in corn syrup and Coca-Cola threads to show that sugar type barely matters in soda because sucrose inverts into the same sugars.

published.title: Scavenging rechargeable lithium cells from the roadside
published.summary: Big Clive shows how to pick up discarded disposable vape devices from the roadside and extract the rechargeable lithium cells inside. He explains why these devices contain the same circuitry as rechargeable ones and how to reuse the cells.
published.why_hn: Used as the explanation behind the free-lithium-cell scavenging idea in threads about vapes and battery reuse.

published.title: Second Reality by Future Crew (pc demo)
published.summary: A capture of Second Reality, the real-time audiovisual demo by Future Crew first shown at Assembly 1993, recorded from a 486DX2-66 with a Gravis Ultrasound. It showcases the peak of early 1990s PC demoscene techniques.
published.why_hn: HN points to it as one of the best and most formative early PC demos, a touchstone of demoscene history.

published.title: Sam Aaron live coding an ambient electro set w/ Sonic Pi
published.summary: Sam Aaron live codes an ambient electronic set using Sonic Pi, the music programming environment he created. The performance shows code driving music in real time.
published.why_hn: Offered as an example of live-coded music and a fun entry point to Sonic Pi.

published.title: Is Meat Really that Bad?
published.summary: A Kurzgesagt animated explainer on the climate and environmental cost of meat. It covers how beef drives deforestation and emissions, and how this compares with plant-based foods.
published.why_hn: HN commenters cite it as a clear, well-sourced summary of why meat, especially beef, has such a large environmental footprint.

published.title: Meeting my hero! Sailing legend Sven Yrvind
published.summary: Sam Holmes Sailing visits sailing legend Sven Yrvind and tours his boat, covering the man and his small-boat design philosophy.
published.why_hn: HN recommends it as an accessible introduction to Yrvind and his minimalist boat ideas.

published.title: Republic, Lost (my favorite version)
published.summary: Lawrence Lessig's 2011 Berkeley book talk based on Republic, Lost, arguing that money in politics creates institutional corruption in Congress. He calls it his favorite version of the talk.
published.why_hn: HN people point to it as a starting place for understanding how money corrupts American government.

published.title: Ochko123 - How the Feds Caught Russian Mega-Carder Roman Seleznev
published.summary: A Black Hat USA 2017 briefing by the prosecutors who caught Russian carder Roman Seleznev. It covers the electronic evidence collected, the international trail, and how he was located and arrested.
published.why_hn: Pointed to as a true-crime story of cybercrime investigation, usually in passing.

published.title: Hacking with Andrew and Brad: tip.golang.org
published.summary: A roughly hour-long live hacking session in which Go team members Andrew Gerrand and Brad Fitzpatrick write the new version of tip.golang.org, the site serving leading-edge Go documentation. It is unedited pair programming on a real Go project.
published.why_hn: HN people point to it as a rare chance to watch skilled developers write real code live, pair programming and explaining as they go.

published.title: 21st Century Jet - Building the Boeing 777 - Full Episode 1
published.summary: The first episode of the 1996 PBS documentary series on the creation of the Boeing 777. It follows the design, build and certification process, including meetings with subcontractors.
published.why_hn: Cited in threads on Boeing and engineering management as a long, interesting look at how a modern airliner was built.

published.title: Millennials Don't Exist! Adam Conover at Deep Shift
published.summary: Adam Conover's talk at a millennial marketing conference argues that generations are an unscientific, condescending idea and that millennials do not exist as a real category. The description notes that researcher Jean Twenge later said he misrepresented some of her work.
published.why_hn: HN commenters cite it when arguing that generational labels are marketing inventions used to belittle groups.
